My tendons strengthened not through shock, but through consistent, low-impact load. My aerobic base, which I had been neglecting in favor of anaerobic bursts, finally deepened. I was building a foundation, not just a facade.

I stopped thinking about the clock. I started thinking about the run. I started to enjoy the quiet. I started to notice that the miles that used to feel like a punishment now felt like a meditation. I was no longer running *toward* a finish line; I was running *through* the experience.

And then, the magic happened.

It wasn’t a sudden epiphany. It was a gradual realization. One day, I went out for a "moderate" run, a pace I used to reserve for my harder days. I felt good. I felt strong. I felt… fast. I checked my watch, and the splits were lower than I had run in months. I didn’t push. I didn’t strain. I just ran.

I realized that speed is not something you grab; it’s something you uncover. It’s a byproduct of efficiency. When you stop wasting energy on tension, on poor form, on unnecessary aggression, the speed emerges on its own. It’s like water finding its level. You don’t push water downhill; you just remove the obstacles.

The day I ran my sub-four marathon, I didn’t feel like a hero. I felt like a student who had finally learned the basics. I didn’t go out trying to kill the clock. I went out trying to stay relaxed. I kept my effort level steady, my breathing deep, my form loose. I trusted the work I had done in the slow miles. I trusted the foundation.

When I crossed the finish line, I was exhausted, but not destroyed. I was tired, but not broken. And the time? It was 3:58:42.

People ask me what changed. They expect me to tell them about a new pair of shoes, a specific diet, a miracle workout. But the truth is boring. The truth is that I learned to be patient. I learned that the fastest way to go fast is to go slow.

In a world that is obsessed with speed, with instant gratification, with "more, more, more," it is a radical act to slow down. To accept that growth is not a sprint, but a marathon. To understand that strength is not just about power, but about sustainability. To realize that the most powerful thing you can do is to let go of the need to force outcomes, and instead focus on the process.

I am 41. I ran my first sub-four. And I am slower than I was five years ago. My five-kilometer time is worse. My mile time is worse. But my marathon time is better. Because I learned that life, like running, is not about how hard you can push, but how well you can endure. It’s not about how fast you can go, but how far you can go, without breaking.

So, if you’re chasing a goal, and you feel stuck, maybe the answer isn’t to push harder. Maybe it’s to slow down. Maybe it’s to breathe. Maybe it’s to trust that the speed will come, if you let it.

Because the fastest runners aren’t the ones who are running the fastest. They’re the ones who are running the most efficiently. And efficiency, I’ve learned, is born from stillness. From slowness. From the quiet, unglamorous work of letting go.

prompt: For my climbing blog: why bouldering gyms have become the new bars for people in their late twenties. I have theories (no alcohol required, built-in conversation starters, nobody looks at their phone) but want the essay to actually figure out what's going on rather than just list them.
chosen:
The bar used to be the default setting for late-twenties socializing because it lowered the barrier to entry. You could sit in silence, drink in peace, and still be surrounded by people. It was a container for proximity without the pressure of performance.

But the bar has broken. The silence is no longer peaceful; it is competitive. The phone has replaced the drink as the primary object of focus. And the conversation, when it happens, often feels like a audition for a social circle you aren’t sure you belong to.

Bouldering gyms didn’t replace the bar because they are better for drinking. They replaced it because they solved the specific crisis of the late-twenties: the need for shared focus.

In a gym, you are physically engaged. You are looking at a hold, calculating your weight distribution, and solving a puzzle with your body. This shared attention is the key. When two people are both trying to stick a sequence on a 5.10b, they are not performing for each other. They are collaborating on a problem. The conversation that follows—"Did you see how he got that heel hook?" or "My left hand slipped on that crimp"—is concrete. It is grounded in the immediate, shared experience. It is not small talk. It is debriefing.

This is why the phone disappears. You cannot hold a phone while you are hanging from a wall. You cannot check Instagram while you are spotting a friend on a problem three feet higher than their head. The environment physically enforces presence.

There is also a subtle shift in status. In your early twenties, status in a bar was often about who was buying rounds, who was dancing, who was attracting the most eyes. In your late twenties, that performance becomes exhausting. Bouldering offers a different kind of status: competence. It is visible, immediate, and egalitarian. A person with a law degree and a person with a graphic design portfolio are equal on the mat. Their value is measured in millimeters of reach and grams of grip strength. For a moment, the noise of careers and titles falls away.

The "no alcohol" factor is less about sobriety and more about clarity. Alcohol blurs the edges of social interaction. It makes people louder, more opinionated, and more prone to misreading cues. Bouldering keeps the interactions crisp. You hang, you spot, you talk for ten minutes, and you go to the next problem. The social unit is the problem, not the hour. This fits the late-twenties lifestyle, which is often fragmented by work, dating, and the slow accumulation of responsibilities. There is less time for a three-hour dive into a bar. There is time for a 45-minute session where you leave feeling physically accomplished and socially connected.

It is not that people have stopped drinking. It is that they have realized the bar is no longer doing the job. The job is no longer just to be around people. The job is to be *with* them, in a way that feels real. The gym provides that. It provides a structure for connection that doesn’t require you to pretend you are having a great time when you are just tired. It allows you to be tired, and to be tired together, and to solve something hard, and to walk out into the evening air feeling like you did something.

The bouldering gym isn’t just a place to climb. It’s a place to *be*. For the late-20s professional, it offers a solution to the modern social dilemma: How do you connect with others without the noise of alcohol, the distraction of phones, and the pressure of small talk?

prompt: why spreadsheets are underrated as a creative medium. go
chosen:
We treat spreadsheets as utility. They are the accounting ledger, the inventory tracker, the tax form. We see them as containers for data, not as a canvas for expression. This is a category error.

A spreadsheet is a grid. It is the most fundamental structure of visual art. It is the pixel lattice, the musical staff, the chessboard. When you strip away the financial jargon and the auto-formatting, you are left with a coordinate system where logic meets layout.

**The Medium is the Logic**

In painting, you mix colors. In a spreadsheet, you mix *functions*. This is a creative constraint that yields unexpected results. You are not just placing an object on a canvas; you are defining the rules of how that object exists.

Consider the `IF` statement. It is not just a filter; it is a narrative device. It creates tension. It says: *if this is true, then that happens.* This is the syntax of drama. A well-crafted formula is a poem of cause and effect. When you build a model where a single input cascades through fifty interdependent cells, you are not doing math. You are composing a system. You are watching a story unfold in real-time as you tweak the variables.

**Spatial Rhythm**

The grid provides a rhythm that prose cannot. In a novel, time is linear. In a spreadsheet, time can be spatial. You can arrange dates in columns, metrics in rows, and watch the correlation emerge as a visual pattern.

This is where the creativity spikes. You are not just reporting numbers; you are choreographing their relationship. The alignment of a header, the indentation of a sub-total, the color coding of a variance—these are aesthetic choices. They guide the eye. They create hierarchy. A masterful spreadsheet is a piece of information design. It is typography applied to logic.

**The Joy of the Broken Link**

There is a specific, visceral thrill in the spreadsheet that is absent in other creative mediums: the fragility of the system.

In a word processor, if you delete a paragraph, you can undo it. In a spreadsheet, if you delete the cell that fifty other formulas depend on, the whole structure collapses into `#REF!`. This is not a bug; it is a feature. It forces a respect for structure. It makes you an architect, not just a builder. You must think about load-bearing walls. You must consider the integrity of the whole.

This constraint creates a kind of tension that is creatively productive. It makes the solution feel earned. When the model finally runs clean, when the errors vanish and the numbers align, there is a satisfaction that is purely structural. It is the feeling of a building standing.

**Why It’s Underrated**

Spreadsheets are underrated because they are invisible. They do not have the cultural prestige of the novel, the film, or the gallery painting. They are associated with drudgery. But this is a bias of context, not of medium.

A musician does not think a piano is a drudge because it is also a tool for practice. A writer does not think a word processor is a drudge because it is also a tool for editing. We should stop thinking of the spreadsheet as a tool for *work* and start seeing it as a tool for *thinking*.

It is a medium for building systems. For modeling reality. For visualizing logic. It is underrated because we are not taught to be creative with it. We are taught to be compliant with it.

But the grid is waiting. The functions are ready. The logic is open. All you have to do is start building.

prompt: Write an essay questioning whether "screen time" is even a meaningful category anymore. Reading a novel on a Kindle, video calling grandma, and doomscrolling all count the same, which seems absurd.
chosen:
We have reached a point where the metric "screen time" is so blunt it has stopped measuring anything useful. It is like a doctor diagnosing a patient based solely on the fact that they are breathing. The number of hours you spend looking at a glass rectangle is no longer a proxy for cognitive load, social isolation, or attention span. It is just... time.

The problem with the current cultural panic over screens is that it treats the interface as the content. It assumes that the mechanism of delivery dictates the quality of the experience. But a Kindle does not turn a novel into a slot machine. A video call does not turn conversation into a dopamine hit. The medium has become so ubiquitous and so varied that the binary of "screen" versus "non-screen" has collapsed into noise.

Consider the absurdity of the equivalence. In most parental control apps and health dashboards, reading *War and Peace* on an e-reader counts the same as scrolling through TikTok. Both are pixels. Both are light. Both are data. But the cognitive architecture required for one is the opposite of the other. Reading a novel demands sustained, linear attention. It requires holding a plot in working memory, synthesizing character motivations, and engaging in deep, slow processing. It is an act of construction. Doomscrolling is an act of consumption. It relies on variable ratio reinforcement schedules—the same mechanics used in gambling—to keep the user engaged through short, unpredictable bursts of novelty. It is passive, fragmented, and designed to prevent deep thought.

To group these activities under a single header is to commit a category error. It is like grouping "sleeping" and "working" under the category of "being in a bed." The physical state is the same; the internal reality is not.

This confusion stems from a technological lag in our vocabulary. We still think of screens as windows or doors, when they are actually environments. A smartphone is not a tool you pick up and put down; it is a room you walk into. The quality of that room depends entirely on what you bring into it. If you bring a library, you are in a library. If you bring a casino, you are in a casino. The glass wall doesn’t change the nature of the activity; it just changes the texture.

The real issue is not the screen, but the attention. And attention is not a resource measured in minutes, but in quality. Ten minutes of focused, intentional engagement with a screen can be more restorative than two hours of mindless staring. Conversely, two hours of deep work on a computer can be more draining than a full day of passive TV watching, because the former demands active executive function while the latter allows the mind to wander.

We need to stop counting hours and start auditing intent. The question is not "How long were you on the screen?" but "What did you do with your mind?" Did you build something? Did you connect with someone? Did you learn? Or did you let an algorithm decide what you should look at next?

The category of "screen time" is a relic of a time when screens were novel, scarce, and clearly distinct from the rest of life. Now that they are the default medium for almost all human activity—work, love, education, entertainment—the metric is obsolete. It is a useless number that tells us nothing about the health of our minds or our relationships.

We need a new vocabulary. We need to talk about *attentional quality*, *cognitive load*, and *intentional engagement*. We need to distinguish between screens that serve us and screens that consume us. But until we make that distinction, we are just counting breaths and calling it health.

**The Pixel Paradox: Why "Screen Time" Has Become a Useless Metric**

In the early days of the smartphone era, the phrase "screen time" carried a distinct, almost moralistic weight. It was a warning label, a red flag indicating that a user was neglecting the physical world in favor of the digital one. Parents worried about their children’s eyesight; sociologists warned of social isolation; productivity gurus railed against the fragmentation of attention. The metric was simple: minutes spent staring at a rectangular slab of glass and silicon. However, as technology has woven itself into the fabric of every human interaction, the category of "screen time" has become increasingly incoherent. To lump a novel read on a Kindle, a video call with a grandmother, and a mindless scroll through a social media feed into a single statistical bucket is not just imprecise; it is absurd. It is a categorization error that obscures more than it reveals, rendering the metric meaningless in an age of digital ubiquity.

The fundamental flaw in the "screen time" metric is its total blindness to context. It treats all pixels as equal, regardless of the cognitive load they impose or the emotional resonance they carry. Consider the act of reading. For centuries, reading was associated with paper, silence, and deep focus. Today, a significant portion of literary consumption happens on e-readers like the Kindle. When a reader spends two hours on a Kindle, their screen time clock ticks up, yet their brain is engaged in a high-order cognitive activity: narrative immersion, empathy building, and sustained attention. To equate this state with the passive, fragmented, and often anxiety-inducing nature of "doomscrolling" is a category mistake. The former is an act of consumption that often enriches the mind; the latter is often an act of compulsion that depletes it. By counting them as the same, we lose the ability to distinguish between engagement and distraction.

This dichotomy becomes even more stark when we consider communication. Video calling a loved one is, by definition, screen time. Yet, it is also one of the most profound ways humans maintain connection across distance. When a grandchild video chats with a grandmother, the screen is not a barrier; it is a bridge. The interaction involves eye contact, tone of voice, and shared emotion. To label this interaction merely as "screen time" strips it of its social significance. It reduces a vital act of human bonding to a data point in a health app, suggesting that the user is "away" from reality, when in fact, they are deeply present in a digital relationship. If we continue to use "screen time" as a proxy for "unhealthy behavior," we risk stigmatizing the very tools that allow us to maintain our most important relationships in a globalized world.

Furthermore, the metric fails to account for the active vs. passive nature of digital interaction. Doomscrolling is largely passive; the user is a recipient of algorithmically curated content, often designed to trigger negative emotional responses or infinite loops of low-value information. In contrast, using a tablet to edit a video, coding a program, or even playing a complex strategy game requires active agency, problem-solving, and skill. These activities may involve more intense focus and longer periods of screen exposure than a casual text message, but they are cognitively different from passive consumption. By aggregating all these activities under one umbrella, we ignore the spectrum of digital literacy and engagement. We treat a surgeon using a digital interface for a procedure the same as a teenager mindlessly swiping through TikTok, ignoring the vast gulf in intent, skill, and outcome.

The persistence of the "screen time" metric is likely less about its analytical value and more about its cultural utility. It provides a simple, quantifiable way to feel in control of a complex technological landscape. Telling a child to "put down the screen" is an easier directive than explaining the nuances of algorithmic manipulation, digital citizenship, or mindful consumption. For parents and educators, the metric offers a false sense of security; if the number is low, the behavior is deemed "safe." This simplicity, however, comes at the cost of nuance. It prevents us from asking the harder, more important questions: *What* are you doing on the screen? *Why* are you doing it? *How* does it make you feel?

As screens become less distinct from the physical world—through augmented reality, always-on wearables, and ambient computing—the very concept of "screen time" will likely become obsolete. We are moving toward a world where the digital and physical are seamlessly integrated, making the binary of "on screen" vs. "off screen" a relic of a transitional era. In this future, the question will not be how many hours we spend looking at a display, but how effectively we use the digital tools at our disposal to enhance our lives, relationships, and work.

In conclusion, "screen time" is a vestigial metric. It is a blunt instrument trying to measure a nuanced reality. Reading a novel on a Kindle, video calling a family member, and doomscrolling are fundamentally different acts with different psychological and social implications. To group them together is to misunderstand the nature of modern digital life. It is time to retire the "screen time" statistic and replace it with a more sophisticated understanding of digital engagement—one that values quality over quantity, context over duration, and meaning over mere minutes.

prompt: Write a mock-serious essay defending the walk-off as the most dramatically perfect ending in all of sport, better than the buzzer-beater, better than penalties.
chosen:
The walk-off is not a failure of courage. It is the ultimate assertion of dominance. It is the moment the scoreboard becomes irrelevant because the outcome has already been decided by the sheer weight of inevitability.

In sports, we are conditioned to value the narrow margin. We rewatch the buzzer-beater in slow motion, frame by frame, celebrating the hair’s breadth between victory and defeat. We hold our breath during a penalty shootout, suspending reality in the hope that a single kick will tilt the scales. These moments are thrilling because they are fragile. They rely on chance, on a split-second lapse in attention, on the specific geometry of a ball hitting a post or a goalkeeper diving the wrong way.

The walk-off strips away the fragility. It tells the opponent, and the audience, that the game is over. Not because the clock has run out, but because the gap in quality is so vast that continuation is a waste of everyone’s time. It is a statement of such profound confidence that it borders on the theatrical.

Consider the psychology of the walk-off. The team that walks off knows something the team left behind does not: they have already won. The remaining minutes are merely administrative. They are the time it takes to pack up the equipment, to stretch, to drink water, to discuss dinner. This is the antithesis of the anxiety that defines modern competition. The buzzer-beater is born of desperation; the walk-off is born of certainty.

There is a moral clarity to the walk-off that the penalty shootout lacks. A penalty shootout is a lottery. It reduces complex athletic prowess to a single binary event: goal or no goal. It is arbitrary. The walk-off, however, is a cumulative truth. It is the sum of every possession, every defensive stand, every strategic decision that led to this moment. It is not a fluke; it is a verdict.

Critics will say the walk-off is disrespectful to the opponent. They will say it robs the losing team of the dignity of a full contest. This is a misunderstanding of the nature of competition. The opponent has already lost. To force them to play on, to force them to chase a deficit that is mathematically and physically impossible to overcome, is not respect. It is torture. It is asking a man to run a marathon when his legs have been broken. The walk-off is an act of mercy. It says, "We have done what needed to be done. Let us go."

In a world obsessed with close races and photo finishes, the walk-off is a radical act. It rejects the idea that all games must be tight to be meaningful. It asserts that some victories are so large they cannot be contained by the boundaries of the field or the limits of the clock. It is the most honest ending in sport because it reflects the reality of the game as it actually was, not as we wish it to be.

The buzzer-beater is a miracle. The penalty shootout is a gamble. The walk-off is a fact. And in the end, facts are far more powerful than either.

prompt: Compose an essay on the ethics of reading someone's old public posts, say, a job candidate's tweets from 2013. Is the past of the internet fair game?
chosen:
The assumption that the internet is a neutral archive of human thought is a convenient fiction. When we look back at a job candidate’s tweets from 2013, we are not looking at a static record of their character. We are looking at a snapshot of a specific moment in a specific context, stripped of the evolution, apology, or context that usually follows a mistake.

The ethical tension here lies in the mismatch between our sense of time and the machine’s. For humans, the past is processed, integrated, and often forgiven. We grow. We learn. A 22-year-old who posts a thoughtless joke in 2013 is not the same moral agent as the 30-year-old who applied for the job in 2024. The internet, however, does not forgive. It does not forget. It treats 2013 and 2024 with the same algorithmic indifference, placing the past on equal footing with the present.

This creates two distinct ethical problems.

**The Problem of Context Collapse**
Most online speech is performed for a specific audience. In 2013, a tweet about politics or a personal grievance was likely intended for friends, peers, or a niche community. It was not intended for a hiring manager, a landlord, or a future spouse. When we pull those posts out of their original social container and place them in a new one, we commit a form of fraud. We are judging the speaker based on a performance that was never meant for that judge. This is similar to judging a person by their private jokes at a bar, recorded by a friend and played back in a courtroom. The content is the same, but the ethical weight changes entirely because the context has been destroyed.

**The Problem of Stagnation**
If we treat old posts as definitive evidence of character, we are essentially arguing that people do not change. This is a cynical and empirically false view. Most people’s views on religion, politics, race, and social norms shift over the course of their lives. To hold someone to their 2013 views in 2024 is to deny their capacity for growth. It suggests that moral development is a one-time event, occurring in youth, after which the soul is fixed. This is not just ethically problematic; it is intellectually lazy. It replaces the difficult work of understanding who a person *is* now with the easy shortcut of finding out who they *were*.

However, there is a counter-argument: consistency. If a person’s core values are truly fixed, their past posts are a reliable predictor of their future behavior. If someone in 2013 expressed hatred toward a specific group, and they still hold those views, the past is relevant. The problem is that we cannot easily distinguish between a fixed belief and a transient mood without asking the person directly. And if we can ask them directly, we don’t need the tweets.

The solution is not to ban the reading of old posts. That is impossible and undesirable. People have a right to investigate potential partners, employees, and neighbors. The solution is to change how we interpret the data.

We must treat old public posts as *data points*, not *verdicts*. A tweet from 2013 is not a confession; it is a question. It invites a conversation. "I saw you wrote X in 2013. How do you feel about that now?" This shifts the dynamic from judgment to inquiry. It acknowledges that the past is part of the story, but not the whole story.

In the end, the internet is not a mirror; it is a museum. Museums preserve artifacts, but they do not define the living. We must resist the urge to treat the digital past as the present truth. To do so is to demand a level of permanence from human beings that they do not possess. We are fluid, contradictory, and evolving. Our past posts are just one of the many drafts in the long process of becoming who we are.

**The Digital Fossil Record: Ethics, Context, and the Right to be Forgotten**

In the early days of the internet, the web was a boundless frontier where anonymity was common and permanence was an afterthought. Users posted with a casual spontaneity, often unaware that their words would be archived by search engines and social media platforms, creating a permanent, searchable fossil record of their thoughts. Today, this digital past has become a tool of scrutiny. From job candidates being vetted for "toxic" tweets from a decade ago to celebrities facing professional repercussions for private jokes made in public, the question arises: Is the past of the internet fair game?

The ethics of reading someone’s old public posts—such as a job candidate’s tweets from 2013—are complex, balancing the interests of employers and the public against the individual’s right to personal growth, privacy, and context.

### The Argument for Scrutiny: Integrity and Public Trust

Proponents of digging into a candidate’s digital history argue that online presence is part of one’s professional identity. In an era where personal branding is paramount, a person’s online footprint can reveal values, judgment, and character traits that a resume cannot. For roles in public relations, journalism, leadership, or education, consistency between one’s public persona and private beliefs may be a legitimate criterion for hiring.

Furthermore, there is an argument for accountability. If a candidate publicly advocates for hate speech, discrimination, or illegal activities, even if it was in the past, it may signal a fundamental misalignment with the organization’s core values or legal compliance standards. Employers have a duty to mitigate risk, and understanding a candidate’s history can help predict future behavior. In this view, the internet is not a "past" that should be ignored, but a continuous narrative of who a person is.

### The Counterargument: Context, Growth, and the Right to Evolve

However, the ethics of this practice are heavily challenged by the argument that humans are not static. People change. The 20-year-old who posts a crude joke or a politically charged opinion in 2013 is not necessarily the same person applying for a senior role in 2024. To judge someone solely on their digital fossil record is to deny them the right to moral and intellectual growth.

This is compounded by the issue of **context**. Online posts are often stripped of their original context. A tweet that seems offensive in isolation may have been part of a nuanced debate, a sarcastic reply to a troll, or a reaction to a specific local event that is no longer salient. Without the full thread, the date, or the cultural moment, employers and the public may misinterpret harmless or even progressive statements as evidence of bias or incompetence.

Moreover, the concept of **proportionality** is key. A minor gaffe or an outdated opinion should not carry the same weight as a sustained pattern of harmful behavior. If we hold individuals to the standard of their worst, most unguarded moment from a decade ago, we create a system where people are permanently penalized for being human. This undermines the principle of rehabilitation and the idea that individuals can learn from their mistakes.

### The Privacy Paradox: "Public" Does Not Mean "For Sale"

A critical ethical distinction must be made between "public" and "fair game." While tweets are technically public, the expectation of privacy has evolved. In 2013, many users did not anticipate that their posts would be used as evidence in employment decisions years later. The scope of who can see these posts has expanded beyond the original audience (friends, family, colleagues) to include recruiters, HR departments, and the general public.

This raises questions about **consent**. Did the user consent to their 2013 posts being used to evaluate their 2024 job application? Likely not. The ethical use of digital history should consider the **reasonable expectations of privacy** at the time the content was posted. If a platform or employer exploits data that was shared with a different set of expectations, it may violate ethical norms of trust and fair dealing.

### Toward a Balanced Ethical Framework

So, is the past of the internet fair game? The answer is not a simple yes or no, but a nuanced "conditionally."

1.  **Relevance and Proportionality**: Employers should focus on recent behavior and statements that are directly relevant to the job. A 2013 tweet about a political candidate should not be weighted more heavily than a 2023 statement about workplace ethics, unless the role specifically involves political advocacy.
2.  **Contextual Understanding**: Evaluators should seek to understand the context of old posts. This may involve looking at the full thread, the user’s subsequent behavior, or even asking the candidate to explain the context during an interview.
3.  **Right to Growth**: Ethical hiring practices should allow room for growth. If a candidate can demonstrate that they have reflected on and changed their views, that evolution should be valued, not penalized.
4.  **Transparency**: Companies should be transparent about how they use digital data in hiring. Candidates should know that their online presence is being reviewed, giving them the chance to manage their digital footprint or address concerns proactively.

### Conclusion

The internet’s permanence has created a moral dilemma. While digital history can offer valuable insights into a person’s character, using it as a definitive judgment tool ignores the complexity of human development. The ethics of reading old public posts require a balance between accountability and compassion. We must reject the notion that the past is forever "fair game" without context. Instead, we should adopt a framework that values growth, respects the evolving nature of privacy, and ensures that individuals are not condemned by their digital fossils. In doing so, we preserve the integrity of the hiring process while honoring the right of every person to learn, change, and move forward.

prompt: Argue that youth sports would be better if we stopped keeping score until age 12. Then, in the same essay, take that argument apart honestly. I coach U10 and genuinely don't know where I land.
chosen:
The case for abolishing scorekeeping in youth sports up to age twelve rests on a simple premise: the adult desire to see a winner is a poison to the child’s desire to learn. When a score is on the board, the game changes. The focus shifts from technique to outcome. A ten-year-old who misses a catch because he was trying to make a highlight reel rather than track the ball is a child who has learned the wrong lesson. Without a score, the pressure to perform for an audience vanishes. The game becomes a laboratory. A striker who misses a shot feels less shame and more curiosity. A defender who loses a duel is asked, "Why did you step that way?" rather than, "Why didn’t you stop that?"

This approach also democratizes participation. In scored games, the natural selection process is brutal. The fastest, strongest, and most coordinated children dominate the ball. The coach, often unconsciously, feeds the ball to the best players because they make the team look good. The other eight children on the field become spectators in their own lives. Without a score, the coach can mandate rotations. Every child gets the ball. Every child gets a chance to fail in a low-stakes environment. The kid who is slow but has good vision gets to play. The kid who is strong but clumsy gets to work on coordination without the immediate feedback of a goal against him. The metric of success becomes improvement, not victory.

Furthermore, removing the score disrupts the toxic culture of adult projection. Parents in the stands often scream at referees or players because the score reflects their own unmet needs. If the scoreboard is blank, the emotional stakes for the adults drop. The game is no longer a referendum on the parent’s parenting skills or the child’s future career. It becomes just a game. Children play more freely when they know the adults are not emotionally invested in the final number. The noise level drops. The coaching becomes more technical. The children can hear each other.

However, this argument collapses under the weight of reality.

First, competition is not a bug; it is the feature. Sports are, by definition, competitive. To remove the score is to remove the essence of the activity. A soccer match without a goal is a pickup game of keep-away. It lacks structure. It lacks tension. For many children, the tension is the point. They want to see if they can win. They want to feel the surge of adrenaline that comes from being down by one goal with five minutes left. By denying them that experience, we are denying them a fundamental human emotion. We are trying to sanitize an activity that is inherently messy and hierarchical.

Second, the "democratization" argument is often a coach’s ego, not a child’s right. While it is true that the best players dominate, the worst players are often dominated by the best players in a scored game. But in an unscored game, the best players still dominate. They just do it in a way that is harder to quantify. The coach who insists on equal touches is often doing so to avoid the discomfort of making tough decisions. It is easier to rotate the ball than to tell a parent that their son is not ready for the starting lineup. Unscoored games can become a hiding place for coaches who are unwilling to manage performance levels. The child who is significantly less skilled may actually prefer the scored game, because it gives them a clear target: get better so you can matter. In an unscored game, they may never know if they are getting better because there is no feedback loop.

Third, age twelve is an arbitrary and biologically problematic cutoff. Puberty does not wait for a calendar. Some ten-year-olds are physically and emotionally ready for high-stakes competition. Some twelve-year-olds are still developing basic coordination. A blanket rule ignores the individual. A gifted ten-year-old who is denied the chance to compete against his peers in a scored environment may become bored, resentful, and disengaged. He may quit the sport entirely because the environment feels infantilizing. On the other hand, a late-blooming twelve-year-old who has been in unscored games for two years may be thrown into a scored environment with zero experience in managing pressure, leading to a crisis of confidence.

Finally, the assumption that adults are the primary source of toxicity is flawed. Children are ruthless. They judge each other. They mock mistakes. In a scored game, the score provides an objective standard for judgment. In an unscored game, the judgment becomes more personal and arbitrary. "You missed that easy pass" is a critique that happens regardless of the scoreboard. Without the score, there is no shared reference point for what "good" looks like. The coach becomes the sole arbiter of quality, which can be even more oppressive than the score.

The truth is that scorekeeping is a tool, not a moral failing. A coach who uses the score to punish or to create anxiety is a bad coach. A coach who uses the score to teach resilience, strategy, and emotional regulation is a good coach. The problem is not the scoreboard; it is the culture surrounding it. We can keep the score and teach children how to lose, how to win, and how to care about the process more than the result. Or we can remove the score and discover that children still care about winning, they just care about it in less visible, less constructive ways.

For a U10 coach, the honest answer is that you do not need to abolish the score to save the children. You need to change the weight you place on it. Keep the score, but de-emphasize it in the post-game. Praise the effort, the positioning, and the courage, not the result. If the team lost 0-1, the game was not a failure. If the team won 10-0, the game was not a triumph. The score is data, not destiny. That is a harder lesson to teach than removing the scoreboard, but it is the one that will serve them when they are adults.

**The Case for the Scoreless Decade: And Why It’s Harder Than It Looks**

You are standing on the sideline at a U10 soccer match, watching two eight-year-olds scream at each other over a missed pass, while a parent in the stands checks their phone, waiting for the final whistle to update the league standings. You’ve likely felt the tension of that moment: the disconnect between the joy of movement and the anxiety of winning.

The argument for stopping scorekeeping in youth sports until age 12 is compelling, intuitive, and widely shared by educators and child psychologists. If we accept the premise that early childhood is a time for exploration rather than evaluation, then removing the scoreboard seems like the logical next step. Here is the case for why we should stop keeping score.

### The Argument: Why We Should Stop Keeping Score

**1. Protecting Intrinsic Motivation**
Psychological research consistently shows that when children are praised or rewarded for outcomes (winning, scoring) rather than processes (effort, improvement, fun), their intrinsic motivation to participate erodes. When a U10 player scores a goal, their immediate thought is often, *"I won,"* rather than *"I enjoyed kicking the ball."* By removing the score, we shift the focus back to the activity itself. We teach children that they are athletes because they love the game, not because they need to validate their worth through a numerical advantage.

**2. Reducing Developmental Pressure**
At ages 6–12, children are in a critical stage of physical and cognitive development. Their bodies are growing unevenly; some are already tall and strong, while others are still small. In a scored environment, physical maturity often correlates directly with performance. The bigger kid gets the ball, scores, and feels good. The smaller kid gets overwhelmed, makes mistakes, and feels bad. This creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where early physical advantages become entrenched confidence gaps. Without a score, the "winner" is no longer the team with the best big kid, but the team that communicated well, worked hard, and showed sportsmanship. This levels the playing field in terms of psychological safety.

**3. Fostering True Sportsmanship**
When the score is on the line, children (and adults) tend to prioritize winning over integrity. We’ve all seen the dirty block, the excessive foul, or the refusal to shake hands. When there is no score, the only metric left is how you played. This encourages cooperation. In unstructured play or scoreless leagues, you often see more passing, more encouragement, and more inclusion of quieter players because the goal isn’t to beat the other team, but to play *with* your teammates.

**4. Preventing Early Burnout**
The "win at all costs" mentality is a primary driver of youth sports dropout. By age 10, many children have already experienced the sting of repeated failure in a high-pressure, scored environment. Removing the score for two more years buys time for children to find their own relationship with sport—whether that’s competitive, recreational, or purely physical—without the weight of expectation.

---

### The Takedown: Why It’s Not That Simple

Now, let’s take that argument apart. As a coach, you know the reality isn’t as clean as the theory. Here is why stopping scorekeeping until 12 might actually do more harm than good, or at least, why it’s a flawed solution to a complex problem.

**1. It Removes a Vital Learning Tool: Handling Loss and Winning**
Winning and losing are not just outcomes; they are life skills. How does a child learn to handle defeat if they never experience it in a structured, low-stakes way? How do they learn the euphoria of overcoming adversity to win? By shielding children from the scoreboard until 12, we may be creating a generation that is unprepared for the inevitable losses they will face in later life. The U10/U12 transition becomes a sudden, jarring shock. Suddenly, the score matters. Suddenly, the parent’s face changes. Suddenly, the coach’s feedback is tied to results. This abrupt shift can be more damaging than gradual exposure.

**2. It Can Undermine Competitive Drive**
Not every child wants to play for the sake of playing. Some are naturally competitive. They thrive on challenge. They want to test their skills against others. For these children, removing the score can feel like removing the game. It can make sports feel like a prolonged warm-up that never leads to the main event. By denying them the structure of competition, we may inadvertently push these high-motivation athletes toward other activities (like video games or individual sports) that offer clear metrics of success and progression. We risk creating a false dichotomy: either you play for fun (no score) or you play for competition (score), when in reality, most humans want both.

**3. It Ignores the Parental and Community Context**
Youth sports are embedded in a social ecosystem. Parents invest time, money, and emotion. Coaches are often volunteers operating on goodwill. Without a score, what is the narrative? How do we celebrate progress? How do we measure team improvement? For many parents, the score is a simple, objective way to gauge their child’s development. Without it, feedback becomes more subjective, which can lead to more conflict, not less. "Why did my kid sit on the bench?" becomes a harder question to answer when there’s no score to justify tactical decisions. The score provides a clear, neutral framework for discussion. Removing it doesn’t eliminate conflict; it just makes it harder to manage.

**4. It’s a Blunt Instrument for a Nuanced Problem**
The real issue with U10 sports isn’t the score itself—it’s *how* we use it. A scoreboard is just a tool. The problem arises when coaches, parents, and kids fixate on it as the sole measure of success. Instead of removing the tool, we should be retraining how we use it. We can keep score but emphasize effort, teamwork, and individual growth in our feedback. We can have "scoreless" practices to focus on skill, but keep games scored to teach competition. Eliminating scorekeeping entirely is like banning cars because some people drive recklessly. It solves the symptom (anxiety about winning) but ignores the root cause (poor coaching, parental pressure, and lack of emotional resilience training).

**5. The "Age 12" Arbitrary Cutoff**
Why 12? Is it because of puberty? Because of cognitive development? There’s no hard scientific line where a 12-year-old suddenly understands the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation any better than a 10-year-old. Development is individual. Some 8-year-olds are emotionally mature enough to handle competition with grace; some 12-year-olds are still deeply insecure. A blanket policy based on age ignores the individuality of the child.

### Where Do You Land?

You don’t have to choose between "all score" and "no score." You can be the coach who bridges the gap.

Consider a hybrid approach:
- **Keep the score, but change the narrative.** In post-game talks, never lead with the result. Lead with effort, communication, and individual improvement. Make the score a footnote, not the headline.
- **Introduce "scoreless" games occasionally.** Once a month, have a game where the score doesn’t count. Focus entirely on passing, positioning, and fun. Let kids experience the freedom of unstructured play within a structured setting.
- **Teach resilience explicitly.** Use losses as teaching moments. Ask, *"What did we learn today that we didn’t know yesterday?"* rather than *"Why did we lose?"*
- **Educate parents.** Host a preseason meeting where you clearly state your philosophy: "We care about development more than the record. If you want a pure competitive environment, this may not be the right team for your child."

The goal isn’t to remove the scoreboard. It’s to ensure the scoreboard doesn’t remove the joy. You don’t need to stop keeping score until 12. You need to start keeping *perspective* from age 6.

You’re not wrong to feel torn. The ideal world where children play purely for joy is beautiful, but the real world where they need to learn to compete, lose, and win is just as real. Your job isn’t to choose one. It’s to hold both in balance.

prompt: Op-ed, maybe 700 words: the group chat has quietly replaced the town square, the dinner party and the family phone call, and nobody voted for that.
chosen:
The notification sound is a soft, synthetic chirp. It is designed to be gentle, to slip under the radar of your attention, to suggest that something is waiting for you without demanding that you drop everything to answer it. But it works. You look down. You see three messages from the "House Holders" group. Then two from the "Book Club." Then a single, urgent question from a colleague about a deadline.

In the span of four minutes, you have not spoken to another human being. You have not seen a face, heard a breath, or felt the texture of a handshake. You have, however, consumed the emotional labor of three different social circles. You have processed jokes, grievances, logistical updates, and passive-aggressive silence. You have done this while standing in the middle of your kitchen, holding a spatula, while the eggs burn.

This is the new town square. It is always open. It is always crowded. And nobody voted for it.

For centuries, public discourse and private intimacy had distinct architectural homes. The town square was physical, bounded by stone and time. You went there to hear the news, to argue with the baker, to watch the mayor. If you didn’t go, you missed out. The dinner party was a temporary structure, a bubble of shared attention that dissolved when the last guest left. The family phone call was a thread of voice, fragile and fleeting, connecting two isolated points in space.

The group chat has collapsed all of these distinct spaces into a single, infinite, scrollable void. It is the town square because it contains the town’s noise: the local news, the political rants, the complaints about the neighbors. It is the dinner party because it is where the in-jokes live, where the tribe signals its cohesion through shared memes and inside references. It is the family call because it is where the mundane logistics of life are negotiated, often with a latency that allows for overthinking rather than spontaneity.

The problem is not that we communicate more. The problem is that we have lost the boundaries that made communication sustainable.

In a physical room, social pressure is immediate and reciprocal. If you talk over someone, they look at you. If you are boring, people check their watches. The feedback loop is fast, visceral, and self-correcting. In a group chat, the feedback loop is delayed, fragmented, and often absent. You can send a message into the void and never know if it landed, if it was read, or if it was mocked. This creates a unique kind of anxiety: the anxiety of the read receipt. The anxiety of the "seen" status. The anxiety of typing in a text field, deleting it, retyping it, and deleting it again, all while wondering if your tone is too sharp or too soft.

Furthermore, the group chat lacks the natural off-switch. The town square closes when the sun goes down. The dinner party ends when the wine runs out. The phone call ends when someone says, "I’ve got to go." The group chat does not end. It lingers. It accumulates. A message sent at 2 a.m. does not wait for morning; it sits there, a small, glowing accusation, waiting for your response. This creates a state of perpetual low-level availability. We are always on call, always ready to perform, always ready to react.

This erosion of boundaries has a cost. It fragments our attention. We no longer engage in deep, sustained conversation; we engage in bursts of reactive commentary. The nuance of face-to-face interaction—the micro-expressions, the pauses, the shared silence—is replaced by the flatness of text. We lose the ability to read the room because there is no room. We lose the ability to let a conversation die naturally because the chat log preserves every dead end, every awkward joke, every unresolved tension.

The irony is that the group chat was supposed to bring us closer. It was supposed to make community easier, more accessible, more inclusive. Instead, it has made community more exhausting. It has turned social life into a second job, one with no pay, no breaks, and no end of shift.

We did not vote for this. We did not sit down and decide that we wanted our public square to be a digital stream of consciousness that never stops. We simply adopted a tool that was convenient, and the tool reshaped us. We are now citizens of a space that is everywhere and nowhere, a space that demands our constant attention but offers no physical refuge.

The solution is not to throw away our phones. That is a fantasy. The solution is to reclaim the architecture of our social lives. We need to treat the group chat for what it is: a tool for logistics, not a home for intimacy. We need to resist the urge to respond to every ping. We need to let the chats sit unread for hours, or days, or weeks. We need to remember that not every message requires a reply. We need to seek out the physical, the bounded, the temporary. We need to go to the actual town square. We need to sit in a room with other people and look at their faces. We need to make a phone call and hear the breath at the end of the line.

The group chat is convenient. It is also a trap. We are walking into it with our eyes open, but we are still walking. It is time to stop.

The town square was loud, messy, and public. You could see who was there. You could leave. If someone started shouting, the crowd would disperse or join in, and the event would end when the sun went down. The dinner party was intimate, structured, and present. You looked people in the eye. You heard the pause before the answer. The family phone call was a bridge, imperfect and fleeting, but it connected two people across a distance with a shared, real-time presence.

None of these are gone. But for a large swath of the population, they have been displaced by the group chat. It is a quieter, more persistent, and more insidious replacement. And the most unsettling part is that no one elected it. There was no referendum on the dissolution of public space, no ballot on the privatization of family time. It simply happened, driven by the convenience of a feature that was designed to keep us online, not to hold our lives together.

The group chat is a hybrid of all three, but it captures the worst of each. It has the permanence of the town square without its accountability. It has the intimacy of the dinner party without its presence. It has the reach of the phone call without its limitation.

In the town square, a conversation is a performance. You are aware of an audience. In the group chat, there is no single audience. There are twelve, or forty, or two hundred. They are not looking at you. They are looking at their screens. You type a thought, and it sits there, waiting for a reaction that may never come, or a reaction that is delayed by hours, or a reaction that is a single emoji that strips the meaning from the sentence. The feedback loop is broken. You are speaking into a void that occasionally echoes back a fragment.

The dinner party required you to be there. You had to sit, listen, and respond. The group chat requires only that you be aware. It is a low-level hum of social obligation. You do not have to read every message, but you feel the weight of the unread notifications. You do not have to reply, but the silence is interpreted. The social pressure is diffuse and constant. It is the anxiety of being potentially expected, forever.

The family phone call was a ritual. It happened at a set time, or when something important came up. It had a beginning and an end. The group chat has no end. It is a continuous stream of updates, memes, complaints, and fragments of life. It is the background noise of the household. It is where the news is broken, where the plans are made, and where the conflicts are aired. It is a court of public opinion that never adjourns.

The danger is not that the group chat is bad. It is a powerful tool for coordination. It is how friends stay in touch across time zones. It is how families organize holidays. But it is not a substitute for the things it has replaced. It cannot hold the weight of a serious conversation. It cannot carry the nuance of a shared meal. It cannot provide the closure of a finished call.

The group chat is a place where everything is recorded. In the town square, words are spoken and gone. In the dinner party, memory is fallible. In the group chat, the history is searchable. This creates a different kind of social dynamic. People perform for the record. They edit their messages. They delete them. They are aware that what they say now will be there later, to be re-read, re-interpreted, and re-quoted. This leads to a flattening of expression. The spontaneous, the clumsy, the truly honest, are edited out. What remains is a curated version of the self, posted into the stream.

We have traded the depth of the phone call for the breadth of the chat. We have traded the presence of the dinner party for the convenience of the notification. We have traded the public accountability of the town square for the private, persistent pressure of the group.

And we did not vote for it. We just opened the app. We just tapped the icon. We just let the convenience take over.

The result is a social life that is always on, but never quite on. It is a life of connection that is mediated by a screen, filtered by an algorithm, and constrained by the limitations of text. It is a life where we are always talking, but rarely listening. Where we are always present, but never truly there.

The town square is still there. The dinner party is still possible. The phone call is still available. But they have become optional, extra, even antiquated. The group chat is the default. It is the air we breathe. It is the water we swim in. And like air and water, we take it for granted until we are suffocating in it.

We need to remember that the group chat is a tool, not a place. It is a wire, not a road. We can use it to connect, but we cannot live on it. We need to step away from the screen and into the room. We need to pick up the phone and hear the voice. We need to go to the square and see the faces. We need to reclaim the spaces that require our presence, our time, and our attention.

Not because the group chat is evil. But because it is not enough. It is a shadow of the connection we used to have. And we are living in the shadow, forgetting the light.

prompt: Blog post essay: why I quit my fitness tracker after 6 years and 2.1 million logged steps, and what I noticed about my body once the numbers were gone.
chosen:
For six years, my relationship with my body was mediated by a small black rectangle on my left wrist. I logged 2.1 million steps. I calculated my calorie deficit to the unit. I checked my heart rate variability at 3:00 a.m. to see if I’d slept well enough to justify a coffee.

I wasn’t addicted to fitness. I was addicted to the interface.

The tracker gave me a sense of agency that the actual physical world refuses to grant. If I felt tired, I could check my sleep score. If I felt sluggish, I could look at my activity ring. The data acted as a buffer between me and my biological reality. I could argue with the numbers. I could ignore them. I could feel guilty about them without having to confront the fact that I was just... existing.

When I took the band off, the first thing I noticed was the silence.

Not a peaceful silence. A terrifying one. Without the haptic buzz telling me to stand up, I forgot I was sitting. Without the step count, I had no objective metric for "movement." I didn’t know if I’d walked enough. I didn’t know if I’d rested enough. I was back in the dark, navigating my body by the only instruments that ever really worked: sensation and context.

### The End of Optimization

The biggest shift wasn’t physical; it was epistemic. I stopped asking "What did I do?" and started asking "How do I feel?"

For years, I had conflated data with health. A 10,000-step day was a good day. A 90% sleep efficiency score was a success. But the body is not a spreadsheet. It is a complex, adaptive system that often signals its needs in ways that contradict the metrics.

I would hit my step goal but still feel exhausted. The tracker said I had done enough. My body said I was depleted. For years, I trusted the tracker. I pushed through fatigue because my rings were closed. I ate too much because my calorie counter said I had room. I slept too little because my rest score was "average."

Once the numbers were gone, I couldn’t hide behind them. If I was tired, it was because I was tired. If I was hungry, it was because I was hungry. There was no third party to blame. There was no algorithm to appeal to.

### The Return of Intuition

In the first month, I was anxious. I caught myself reaching for my wrist, expecting a notification. I found myself mentally counting steps while walking to the mailbox. *Is this enough? Am I doing it right?*

But then, slowly, the intuition returned. It was rusty, like a muscle unused for decades. I started noticing the subtle signs I had been ignoring:

*   **The quality of movement.** Instead of chasing a step count, I noticed whether my walk felt light or heavy. Did my shoulders drop when I stepped outside? Did my breath deepen?
*   **The hunger cues.** I stopped eating at set times and started eating when my stomach growled. I stopped drinking water because a reminder popped up and started drinking when my mouth felt dry.
*   **The sleep architecture.** I stopped obsessing over the number of hours. I started paying attention to how I felt when I woke up. Was I groggy? Was I alert? Did I need a nap, and if so, did that nap actually help?

It was less efficient. It was more ambiguous. But it was honest.

### What I Noticed

Without the data, I realized how much of my "health" had been performative. I had been optimizing for the screen, not for the life I was living.

I noticed that I was moving more when I was having fun and less when I was stressed. The tracker had flattened this nuance into a daily number. Now, I could see the pattern. I was a different person on weekends than I was on weekdays. My body responded to joy, not just volume.

I also noticed the anxiety of uncertainty. The tracker had provided a false sense of control. It implied that if I just tracked everything, I could predict and manage my health. But health is not a linear equation. It’s a messy, non-linear process. The uncertainty was uncomfortable, but it was also liberating. I didn’t have to be perfect. I just had to be present.

### The Takeaway

I don’t regret the six years. The data taught me a lot about my habits. It showed me where I was sedentary, where I was overeating, where I was neglecting sleep. It was a useful tool, but it became a crutch.

The lesson isn’t that you should throw away your fitness tracker. It’s that you should know when to take it off.

Use the data to learn, not to live. Use it to identify trends, not to dictate every minute of your day. And when you feel the urge to check the number, pause. Ask yourself: *How does my body actually feel right now?*

The answer might be less precise than the algorithm’s. But it will be truer.
rejected:
For six years, my relationship with my body was mediated by a plastic rectangle on my wrist. I logged 2.1 million steps. I tracked my sleep scores, my resting heart rate, and my blood oxygen levels. I optimized my recovery windows. I chased the green ring.

Then I took it off. Not because I was sick, and not because I was lazy. I took it off because I was tired of being a data point.

The first week was surprisingly uneventful. I didn’t panic. I didn’t stare at my wrist expecting a haptic buzz. I just walked. But the silence that followed was louder than any notification. Without the constant feedback loop, I had to relearn how to talk to my own body. It felt like learning a language I had previously outsourced to a translator.

### The End of Optimization

The most immediate change was the disappearance of performance anxiety. When you track everything, every movement becomes a transaction. Is this walk cardio? Is this nap deep sleep? Is this meal within my macro window? The tracker turns living into a series of inputs and outputs. It demands that you justify your existence through efficiency.

Once the numbers were gone, I stopped asking if I was doing enough. I started asking if I felt good.

There is a profound difference between the two. "Doing enough" is a metric. "Feeling good" is a state. The former is binary and often binary in a way that punishes you for being human. The latter is nuanced, subjective, and forgiving.

### Reconnecting with Somatic Signals

Without the screen, I had to rely on somatic signals—those subtle physical cues that we often ignore in favor of data.

I noticed my joints before they hurt. A slight tightness in my shoulders would prompt me to stretch, not because an app told me my posture score dropped, but because I felt it. I started eating when I was hungry, not when my blood glucose dipped below a certain threshold. I slept when I was tired, not when my sleep score demanded I be in bed by 10:15 PM.

This shift from external validation to internal trust was the hardest part. It felt reckless. Who am I if I don't have a number to back up my health? But the answer was: I am still here. My heart still beats. My legs still move. The data was a crutch, and I had been leaning on it so hard I had forgotten how to stand on my own.

### The Illusion of Control

Fitness trackers promise control. They suggest that if you can measure it, you can manage it, and if you can manage it, you can improve it. It’s a seductive narrative, especially in a world where uncertainty is our constant companion.

But the numbers never told the whole story. They couldn’t tell me that I was stressed, or that I was lonely, or that I was grieving. They could only tell me that my heart rate variability was low. They reduced the complex, messy reality of being a human being to a handful of variables.

When I quit the tracker, I didn’t stop caring about my health. I started caring about it differently. I stopped trying to optimize my life and started trying to live it. I took longer walks, not to hit a step count, but because the air was good and the sky was clear. I rested when I needed to, even if it meant a "poor" sleep score. I moved my body because it felt good, not because it burned the right number of calories.

### What I Gained

I didn’t lose any health by quitting. In fact, I’d argue I gained some. I gained presence. I gained the ability to be in my body without judging it. I gained a sense of peace that no green ring could ever provide.

The 2.1 million steps were real. The health benefits were real. But so was the cost. The cost was my attention. The cost was my ability to trust myself.

If you are wearing a tracker, ask yourself: Does it serve you, or do you serve it? Are you using it to understand your body, or to avoid feeling it?

You don’t need a number to know you’re alive. You just need to be here.

prompt: I'm the person in my family everyone calls for tech help. My mom, my uncle, two neighbors. It's sweet but also exhausting and it's changed my relationships in ways I didn't expect. write an essay about being the family's tech support, the strange power and resentment of it
chosen:
The first time my mother asked me to fix her printer, I was twenty-two. It was a paper jam. I pulled the tray, removed the crumpled sheet, and pressed "resume." She looked at me with a reverence usually reserved for surgeons or priests. "You’re so clever," she said.

That was the beginning.

Being the family tech support is not a job. It is a social position. You are not hired; you are conscripted by proximity and competence. The role defines you in ways that have nothing to do with your career or your interests. To your uncle, you are not a software engineer or a student; you are "the guy who knows about the internet." To your neighbor, you are the person who can make the TV stop saying "No Signal."

The power is immediate and intoxicating. In a world where digital interfaces are increasingly opaque, the person who can see the underlying logic becomes a gatekeeper. You control access to information, to communication, and to entertainment. When you sit at your mother’s kitchen table and plug in a USB drive, the atmosphere changes. She stops talking. She watches your hands. She waits for the screen to light up. For those ten minutes, you are the sun around which the room orbits.

But this power is brittle. It relies entirely on the assumption that you will always be there, always be right, and always be willing. The moment you hesitate, or the moment you say "I don’t know," the reverence curdles into resentment.

The resentment is rarely explicit. It doesn’t come as a complaint that you are annoying. It comes as silence. It comes as your mother sighing when she has to call you because the Wi-Fi dropped, even though you explicitly told her three days ago that the router needed a firmware update. It comes as your uncle not thanking you after you spent two hours troubleshooting his smart home system, instead asking, "So, can you fix my car’s infotainment screen?"

The dynamic shifts the relationship from mutual to transactional. Before you became the tech support, you were family. You shared meals. You exchanged stories. Now, you are a utility. The emotional labor of explaining basic concepts—why you can’t "just update" a phone like a computer, why passwords are case-sensitive, why the cloud is not a physical place—exhausts you in a way that physical labor does not. You are constantly translating a different species of reality. You are speaking a language they do not want to learn, and they expect you to speak it slowly, patiently, and without judgment.

The most damaging effect is the erosion of boundaries. Because you are the "easy" option, you become the default. If something breaks, the first call is always to you. Not to the manufacturer. Not to a professional. To you. This creates a sense of obligation that is difficult to escape. If you say no, you are not just refusing a task; you are refusing a role. You are signaling that you are not as helpful, not as clever, not as family-oriented as you were yesterday.

I remember a Saturday afternoon when I was trying to read a book. My phone rang. It was my neighbor. His printer was jammed again. I had just fixed it for him. I let it ring. I finished the chapter. I went to the kitchen. I made coffee. I did not answer.

When I finally answered, his voice was tight. "It’s jammed again."

"I can’t do it now," I said. "Can you call support?"

There was a long pause. "You’re being difficult," he said.

I hung up. I felt guilty. I felt angry. I felt like I had broken a social contract I never agreed to sign.

The strange thing is that I don’t want to stop helping. I like solving problems. I like the feeling of competence. But I want to help because I choose to, not because I am trapped in a role that defines my worth in terms of my ability to troubleshoot a router.

I have started to set boundaries. I tell my mother to write down the error message before she calls. I tell my uncle to call the manufacturer first. It is hard. It feels rude. But it is necessary.

The power of being the tech support is real, but it is a kind of power that consumes you. It takes your time, your patience, and your peace. It turns family members into clients and friends into users. It is sweet, in the way that a fever is sweet: it feels like vitality, but it is actually a sign that something is wrong.

I am still the person they call. I still fix the printers. I still reset the passwords. But I am trying to remember that I am more than the solution. I am not the fix. I am just the person who happens to know how to use a screwdriver.
rejected:
They call it "the help," but it feels more like a triage center for the digital age. I am the family’s unofficial IT department, a role I did not apply for, did not train for, and certainly did not sign a contract for. My mother, my uncle, and two neighbors from down the street all seem to have independently concluded that I am the only human being in their orbit capable of navigating the treacherous waters of modern connectivity.

It started innocently enough. A question about how to delete a photo. A query about why the TV wouldn’t turn on. But over time, these isolated incidents coalesced into an expectation, a quiet, humming dependency that has fundamentally altered the texture of my relationships. I have become the gatekeeper of information, the interpreter of user interfaces, and the emergency response unit for software glitches. It is a position of immense, invisible labor, and it carries with it a strange, toxic cocktail of power and resentment.

The power is the first thing you notice, and it is intoxicating in its subtlety. In a world where technology is the primary medium for social connection, commerce, and even basic utility, the person who understands the medium holds the keys. When my mother’s email refuses to send, or when my uncle’s streaming service freezes during a crucial moment of a show, I am no longer just their child or their nephew; I am the architect of their reality. I decide when the Wi-Fi resets. I decide which apps are "safe." I decide what is worth upgrading and what should be ignored.

This control is rarely overt. I don’t stand over their shoulders saying, "Do this, and only this." But the dynamic shifts. Conversations that used to be peer-to-peer become teacher-to-student. My opinions on whether to buy a new phone or stick with the old one carry a weight they didn’t before. If I say a particular subscription is a waste of money, they listen. If I say a security update is critical, they comply. I have inadvertently gained a veto power over their daily routines, a soft authority that feels less like leadership and more like stewardship of a fragile ecosystem.

But for every ounce of power, there is a corresponding pound of resentment, and this is where the exhaustion sets in. The resentment is not always directed at me; sometimes, it is directed at the technology itself, but I am the lightning rod for that frustration. When the internet goes down, it is my fault for not "fixing" it sooner. When a new update breaks their tablet, it is my fault for suggesting the update in the first place. I am blamed for the inherent instability of the digital world, a system that is designed to change, break, and reinvent itself, yet I am expected to keep it static and perfect for those who rely on it.

The emotional toll is significant because it changes the nature of intimacy. I find myself holding back, not sharing every tech trend or gadget, fearing that if I show them a new feature, they will demand I install it, explain it, and maintain it. I have become a repository of knowledge that they access only when necessary, not out of curiosity or shared interest. Our conversations about technology are transactional: *Problem here, fix needed, please.* There is little room for the organic, playful exploration of technology that used to exist between us. The joy of discovery has been replaced by the duty of repair.

Moreover, the resentment bleeds into other aspects of our relationships. When I am busy, tired, or simply needing to disconnect, I feel a guilt that is disproportionate to the situation. If I don’t answer the phone immediately, I am not just unavailable; I am failing in my role. If I suggest that they try the troubleshooting steps in the manual, I am perceived as lazy or unhelpful. I am expected to be available on demand, a living, breathing customer service representative who doesn’t take vacations, doesn’t get sick, and never gets tired.

The neighbors add another layer of complexity. They are not blood, but their reliance on me has created a parasitic dynamic that feels less familial and more contractual. I help them because they are kind, and because it is the neighborly thing to do, but the lines are blurry. When I am busy with my own life, their requests feel intrusive. I have learned to say no, but it comes at a cost. I worry about how they perceive me. Am I becoming distant? Am I becoming the person who only helps when it’s convenient? The fear of being seen as selfish for setting boundaries is a constant, low-level hum in the background of my life.

I have started to see this role as a form of emotional labor that is rarely acknowledged. It is not just about fixing the router; it is about managing the anxiety that comes with technological dependence. I am soothing the panic of being disconnected, the frustration of being outpaced by a world that moves faster than they can keep up. I am providing a sense of control in a chaotic environment. And while that is valuable, it is draining to be the sole source of that stability.

So, what is the solution? I don’t have one, yet. I have tried to delegate, to teach them to be self-sufficient. I have printed out instructions, recorded videos, and encouraged them to ask each other. But the inertia of dependency is strong. They prefer the certainty of my expertise to the uncertainty of their own attempts. And I, perhaps, prefer the feeling of being needed, the subtle power of being the one who can make the digital world make sense. It is a comfortable trap.

I am learning to set boundaries, to say, "I can’t help with that right now," or "Let’s look this up together instead of me just fixing it." I am learning to reclaim my role as a son, a nephew, a neighbor, rather than a technician. It is a slow process, one that requires patience and a willingness to let them struggle a little. Because in the end, if I never step back, they will never learn to navigate the world without me. And I will never be free to just be part of the family, rather than its maintenance crew.

The tech will keep breaking. The questions will keep coming. But I am trying to change the answer. Instead of "I’ll fix it," I am trying to say, "Let’s figure it out." It’s a small shift, but it might just be enough to break the cycle of power and resentment, and to restore the balance to our relationships. It’s time to stop being the family’s tech support, and start being just family again.

prompt: I'm 34 and just started powerlifting. Everyone at the gym is either 22 or a 60-year-old who's been doing it forever. Could you write an essay about starting something physical "too late," what you lose and what you might actually gain by not having started at 18? Honest, not a pep talk.
chosen:
The mirror in the gym locker room is a cruel, honest thing. It doesn’t care about your intention, your financial stability, or the fact that you finally have the time to prioritize your health. It only cares about your bone density, your joint history, and the specific, unglamorous reality of your body at thirty-four.

You walk into the powerlifting world, a subculture often defined by raw, primal strength and a demographic that seems to split cleanly into two categories: the twenty-two-year-olds who are peaking just as you are arriving, and the sixty-year-olds who have been hammering iron since the Clinton administration. You are the outlier. You are the middle-aged novice. And the question that keeps you up at night isn’t "Can I do a squat?" It’s "Am I too late?"

The honest answer is: You are late for the version of yourself you imagined at eighteen. You will never be the person who hits a 500-pound squat at twenty because you had the hormonal surge, the zero-negligible injury history, and the neuroplasticity of a teenager. You have lost the window of "cheap" gains. In your teens and early twenties, the body is a sponge. It absorbs volume, recovers from poor sleep, and builds muscle mass with a metabolic efficiency that is biologically impossible to replicate at thirty-four. You are paying a "senior tax" on every rep. Your recovery is slower. Your joints creak. Your center of gravity is different. The twenty-two-year-old next to you can eat a pizza and a beer after a heavy session and wake up with new muscle; you will wake up with a stiff lower back and a question about what you did wrong.
